name: Huang Nubo's bid for Grímsstaðir
challenge: Refused an exemption from the land law
recognition: None sought; land under Icelandic law
cost: About $10 million for the land, with about $200 million of planned investment
story: In 2011 Huang Nubo, a Chinese businessman who founded the property firm Zhongkun Group, tried to buy about 300 square kilometres of wilderness at Grímsstaðir á Fjöllum in north-eastern Iceland, equal to 0.3 per cent of the country. He offered about $10 million for the land, which was partly owned by the government, and planned to spend about $200 million on a tourist resort and a nature reserve. Icelandic law bars large land purchases by people or companies from outside the European Economic Area, a group of European countries that share a single market, so he needed an exemption. Interior Minister Ögmundur Jónasson refused in late 2011. He said an exemption would make the law meaningless and could encourage others to buy up large parts of Iceland. The Social Democrats leaned toward the deal and the minister's Left Greens opposed it, and one Social Democrat member of parliament called the decision crazy. Huang called the minister a racist. In May 2012 a committee of three ministries recommended a smaller deal, a 40-year lease of two to three square kilometres for a hotel and tourist facilities. Huang had said that building one hotel did not interest him. No report says the lease was ever signed.
mechanism: A country can limit who may buy its land by nationality, and here a minister refused to waive that limit. The bid concerned land ownership only, and no sovereignty was on offer.

sources.t: Iceland foils Chinese investor's bid to buy land, Eye on the Arctic
Reykjavik mulls letting Chinese tycoon lease land, AFP via Solar Daily

name: Ras El-Hekma deal
anchor: Ras El-Hekma, on the Mediterranean coast of Egypt.
founder: ADQ, for the government of the United Arab Emirates
cost: $24 billion for development rights plus $11 billion of converted deposits
story: Ras El-Hekma is a stretch of Egypt's Mediterranean coast about 350 kilometres north-west of Cairo. In February 2024 the governments of Egypt and the United Arab Emirates signed a $35 billion agreement over it, with the Emirates represented by a consortium led by ADQ, a state investment fund based in Abu Dhabi. ADQ was to pay $24 billion for the rights to develop the area, and to convert $11 billion of deposits it held into investments in projects elsewhere in Egypt. The plan covers more than 170 million square metres, or about 170 square kilometres, to be built up as a holiday destination, financial centre and free zone, an area with special business and tax rules. Egypt keeps a 35 per cent stake in the development. The UAE's investment minister described it as support for Egypt's economy.
mechanism: The buyer acquired development rights over land in Egypt, and Egypt kept a share of the project. The announcement describes an investment and makes no mention of any transfer of sovereignty.

sources.t: ADQ to invest US$35 billion in Ras El-Hekma, Egypt, Dubai Eye and WAM

name: Dutch purchase of Manhattan
anchor: Manhattan Island; the site of the deal is unknown.
founder: Peter Minuit for the Dutch West India Company
cost: 60 guilders of trade goods, later converted to $24
story: Manhattan, now part of New York City, is famous as the island said to have been bought from the Lenape, its Indigenous people, in 1626 for $24 worth of beads. The buyer was Peter Minuit, director of the colony of New Netherland for the Dutch West India Company, a trading company chartered in the Netherlands. Very little is known about the deal. It rests on two sentences in a single letter of November 1626 by Pieter Schagen, a company board member, who gave the price as 60 guilders of trade goods. A New York historian turned this into $24 in 1844, probably wrongly, and one Amsterdam institute put it at about $1,000 in 2006 money. The goods are not recorded, though a similar deal for nearby Staten Island involved cloth, kettles, axe heads and hoes. Research cited by New York City's Landmarks Preservation Commission suggests the Lenape probably understood the deal as temporary, closer to a lease, and may have seen the 60 guilders as a ceremonial gift sealing an agreement. Manhattan became the site of the Dutch town of New Amsterdam.
mechanism: A trading company treated a payment as buying land outright, while the sellers may have understood it as sharing use. What passed depends on which side's understanding is taken, and the only written record is a Dutch letter.

sources.t: "Purchase" of Manhattan, NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission

name: Nile Trading lease in Mukaya Payam
anchor: Marker is in Lainya County; the exact boundary was not given.
stopped_by: Community opposition and the South Sudanese government
challenge: Local chiefs and officials rejected the lease in 2011
story: Nile Trading & Development is a Texas company that in March 2008 signed a 49-year lease over about 600,000 hectares in Mukaya Payam, a district of Lainya County in what is now South Sudan, for $25,000. According to the Oakland Institute, a California research group that published the contract, the lease gave unencumbered rights to exploit all natural resources on the land, with the possibility of nearly a million acres more. After the Institute's report spread in 2011, the year South Sudan became independent, local people mobilised against it. Chiefs and county authorities protested in July, and in August a committee of chiefs, state legislators and officials went to the capital, Juba, to reject the lease before President Salva Kiir. Kiir replied that the matter should be settled according to their will. The Institute announced that the deal had been effectively stalled. No report says whether it was ever formally cancelled.
mechanism: A lease signed before South Sudan's independence gave a foreign firm wide rights for a small price. It passed no sovereignty, and local opposition reached the president.

sources.t: Success at halting largest foreign land deal in South Sudan, Oakland Institute

name: Bolivian Syndicate in Acre
founder: Bolivian Trading Company of Jersey City
stopped_by: Brazilian opposition and the Treaty of Petrópolis
challenge: Brazil and Peru rejected the lease
recognition: Lease from Bolivia, rejected by Brazil and Peru
cost: 30-year lease; the Syndicate was bought out for £110,000
story: The Bolivian Syndicate was an American and British investment company that in 1901 leased almost total control of Acre, a rubber-rich region in the Amazon then claimed by Bolivia and now part of Brazil. Bolivia, under General José Manuel Pando, signed the lease on 11 June 1901 for 30 years, hoping to protect its hold on a region that was filling with Brazilian settlers. The company's shareholders are reported to have included the king of Belgium and relatives of President William McKinley of the United States. Brazil and Peru claimed the territory too and objected. Brazil withdrew its consul and closed the Amazon's tributaries to Bolivian trade, and the dispute fed the Acre War of 1899 to 1903. Before major fighting between the two armies, the Brazilian diplomat Baron of Rio Branco negotiated a settlement. Under the Treaty of Petrópolis of November 1903 Bolivia gave Acre to Brazil in return for land in Mato Grosso, £2 million and a promised railway. The Syndicate was paid £110,000 to give up its lease.
mechanism: A weak state tried to hold a remote region by leasing it to foreign investors with powers close to a government's. Neighbouring states refused to accept this, and the company was bought out when sovereignty moved by treaty.

name: Sale of the fief of Sark
cost: £6,000 in 1852, less the £4,000 mortgage and £616 13s interest, leaving £1,383
story: Sark, one of the Channel Islands, is a fief, land held from the British monarch, and with the Crown's permission its lordship may be mortgaged or sold. It has changed hands this way. In the 1730s a widow, Susanne le Pelley, bought it. In 1844 the Seigneur, or lord, Ernest le Pelley, needed money to keep a silver mine running and got Crown permission to mortgage the fief for £4,000 to John Allaire, a Guernsey privateer, or licensed ship raider, reputed to be the richest man in Guernsey. Allaire died within two years and his daughter Marie Collings took over the mortgage. The mine closed in 1847 after its deepest gallery collapsed, and the next Seigneur, Pierre Carey le Pelley, could not keep up the payments. When she moved to foreclose, he asked Queen Victoria's permission to sell, and in December 1852 Collings bought the lordship for £6,000 less the loan and interest, which left £1,383 to pay. She never visited and died the next year. Her family still holds the title. Sark's parliament became fully elected in 2008.
mechanism: A lordship with real governing powers could be bought and sold like property, but only with the monarch's consent, and the monarch stayed overlord throughout.

name: Knights of Malta's Caribbean islands
aka: Order of Saint John in the Caribbean
anchor: Saint Kitts, the seat of the governor.
founder: Phillippe de Longvilliers de Poincy for the Knights of Malta
stopped_by: Sold to the French West India Company in 1665
recognition: Proprietor under the French king, by treaty
cost: Price not given; plus a gold crown worth 1,000 écus to each new French king
story: From 1651 to 1665 the Knights of Malta, a Catholic military order, owned four Caribbean islands: Saint Christopher (now Saint Kitts), Saint Croix, Saint Barthélemy and Saint Martin. They came to the order through Phillippe de Poincy, a knight who was also France's governor there and who had defied the French company that ran the islands, driving off the replacement it sent. To keep his post he suggested in 1649 that the order buy them. The Company of the American Islands was failing and it dissolved in 1651, selling its rights. Under a treaty with France two years later the king stayed sovereign, while the knights had full civil and religious authority, could send only French knights as governors, and owed a gold crown worth 1,000 écus to each new king. Poincy ruled as he liked until his death in 1660 and built forts and a grand residence. A rebellion overthrew the order's rule on Saint Croix in 1657 and Caribs attacked Saint Barthélemy. The colonies made no profit and the order still owed France part of the purchase price. Under pressure from the French minister Colbert it sold them in 1665 to the new French West India Company.
mechanism: A religious order bought islands from a bankrupt company. It held ownership and full local government, while the French king kept formal sovereignty.

name: Du Parquet's purchase of Martinique, Grenada and Saint Lucia
challenge: Indigenous islanders fought the settlers on Grenada until 1654
recognition: Proprietor and governor under the French king
cost: 41,500 or 60,000 livres, depending on the source
story: Jacques Dyel du Parquet was a French soldier and the governor of Martinique, who in 1650 bought Martinique, Grenada, Saint Lucia and the Grenadines in the Caribbean from the company he served. The Company of the American Islands was collapsing and selling off its rights. The contract was signed in Paris on 27 September 1650, with the king's approval following in August 1651, and the king made du Parquet governor over the islands he now owned. Sources give different prices: Wikipedia's article on him says 41,500 livres paid in instalments, and its article on the company says 60,000 livres. He had already founded settlements on Grenada and Saint Lucia. On Grenada his settlers fought the indigenous islanders from 1649 until the last resistance was crushed in 1654. He sold Grenada in 1655 to Jean Faudoas, Count of Serillac. On his death in 1658 the king appointed his young son governor of Martinique and Saint Lucia. Another buyer, the sieur Houël, bought Guadeloupe and nearby islands from the company. In April 1664 the king revoked all the sales the company had made to private parties, and a new French West India Company was set up that May.
mechanism: A private buyer acquired islands and then received the governorship from the king, who kept sovereignty. The king later cancelled such sales by decree, which shows that the title lasted only while the Crown allowed it.

name: Lānaʻi and Larry Ellison
founder: Larry Ellison, the latest of several owners
recognition: Private land in the US state of Hawaii
cost: $300 million in 2012 for 98 per cent of the island, land only
story: Lānaʻi is the sixth-largest Hawaiian island, 364 square kilometres, and 98 per cent of it belongs to Larry Ellison, co-founder of the software firm Oracle. He bought that share in June 2012 for $300 million. The other 2 per cent, including the harbour and the homes of the 3,000 residents, belongs to the state or to homeowners. Single owners have held most of the island for over a century. Walter Gibson bought land there for $3,000 in 1863 with Mormon church money, titled it in his own name and was excommunicated, and by the 1870s he held most of the island. By 1907 the rancher Charles Gay owned about half. A law barred the government from selling him so much land, so he got the rest by swapping some Honolulu land for it. James Dole bought the island in 1922 and made it the world's largest pineapple plantation, and it passed to David Murdock in 1985 when he bought the parent company. Ellison has spent an estimated $450 million on one resort there alone.
mechanism: Almost a whole island can be private property while it remains an ordinary part of a county and a US state. The owner controls land, jobs and resorts, and no separate jurisdiction arises from that.

name: Henri Menier's Anticosti Island
anchor: Marker is at the centre of the island.
cost: Price not given; the previous owner paid $101,000 at auction in 1884
story: Anticosti is a 7,943-square-kilometre island in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, Canada, larger than Prince Edward Island, that was bought in 1895 by Henri Menier, the French chocolate millionaire. It had been granted as a seigneury, or feudal estate, to the explorer Louis Jolliet in 1680. A Montreal land company went bankrupt trying to settle it in 1872, and Francis Stockwell, an English businessman who paid $101,000 at auction in 1884, went bankrupt too. Menier wanted a private sports preserve and hoped to make the island a self-supporting estate. He brought in foxes, bison, moose and 220 white-tailed deer, whose descendants now number over 100,000, built a model village at Baie-Sainte-Claire, and in 1900 moved the settlement to Port-Menier, which had a long wharf and a sawmill. He died in 1913 and the island was sold in 1926 to a pulp and paper company. The Quebec government bought it in 1974, and most of its 200 or so people live in Port-Menier today.
mechanism: A foreign buyer could own a whole Canadian island and run it as a personal estate, but it stayed under Canadian law. It ended in public ownership when Quebec bought it.

name: Carlos Casado company in the Paraguayan Chaco
anchor: Puerto Casado, on the Paraguay River.
story: The Carlos Casado company bought huge areas of the Chaco, the dry forest region of western Paraguay, when the Paraguayan state sold public land in the late 19th century. It acquired over 7,800 square kilometres in 1886 and came to hold more than 5 million hectares. It cut quebracho trees to make tannin, a substance used for tanning hides, and built the town of Puerto Casado, founded in 1889, and a railway running 145 kilometres west from the Paraguay River. Mennonite settlers passed through from 1926, and the railway carried soldiers and supplies in the Chaco War. The factory is now shut.
mechanism: A state sold public land to a company on a very large scale. Title passed and Paraguay kept sovereignty, though the company's town and railway served the region.

name: Swazi concessions under King Mbandzeni
anchor: Marker is near Mbekelweni, the royal capital.
founder: Concession seekers from Britain and the Transvaal
recognition: Grants by the Swazi king, later overtaken by the 1884 and 1894 conventions
cost: Paid in gold, cattle and goods
story: During the reign of King Mbandzeni of Swaziland, now Eswatini, which lasted until 1889, white settlers from Britain and the Transvaal, the Boer republic next door, obtained a mass of concessions, grants of rights over land, mining, trade and even administration. Concession seekers crowded his capital at Mbekelweni, and interest grew after gold was found in the Transvaal. He and his officials granted many overlapping rights and were paid in gold, cattle or goods, with advice from 'Offy' Shepstone, a nephew of the Natal colonial official Theophilus Shepstone. According to Wikipedia's account, Boers tricked the king, who could not read or write, into marking papers with a cross after telling him the land concessions were not permanent, though the papers said they were. These concessions led to conventions in 1884 and 1894 that reduced Swaziland's borders and made it a protectorate of the South African Republic, meaning that state took charge of its outside affairs. Mbandzeni is quoted as saying on his deathbed that the Swazi kingship would die with him.
mechanism: Rights over a country can pass piece by piece through many private grants, with no single sale. Here they led to treaties between outside powers that cut the kingdom's borders and ended its independence.

name: Firestone concession in Liberia
challenge: Protests in Liberia against the loan; displaced residents complained to the legislature
cost: Six cents an acre for up to one million acres for 99 years, with a $5 million loan attached
story: In 1926 the American tyre maker Firestone won a 99-year lease on up to a million acres of Liberia, in West Africa, at six cents an acre, wherever in the country it chose. That was 4 per cent of Liberia's territory and nearly 10 per cent of its land then considered arable. Harvey Firestone wanted American-grown rubber because a British scheme had pushed up prices, and Liberia's government wanted American protection from colonial neighbours eager to annex it. After the legislature approved a draft, Firestone added a clause requiring Liberia to take a $5 million loan from his own company, at 7 per cent. The money was meant to pay off debts to British banks, and Liberia agreed under pressure from the US State Department. An American financial adviser then controlled Liberia's budget, and the country could not borrow without the company's consent. The company was largely exempted from taxes and displaced local residents. By 1932 the loan took nearly all government revenue. When Liberia missed a payment, Firestone asked for a warship, and President Roosevelt refused. It still runs the world's largest contiguous rubber farm, at Harbel.
mechanism: Liberia remained independent, but a lease and a loan together gave a company land and a say over state finances. One account calls the result an American protectorate in practice, though no sovereignty formally passed.

sources.t: The 1926 Firestone Concession Agreement, Liberia Past and Present

name: New Zealand Company land purchases
stopped_by: Treaty of Waitangi, land commissions and financial failure
challenge: Spain Land Commission; Wairau Affray of 1843
cost: About a halfpenny an acre, in guns, tools and clothing, for a claimed 20 million acres
story: The New Zealand Company was a British colonising company that claimed to have bought about a third of New Zealand from Māori in 1839. It followed the plan of Edward Gibbon Wakefield, who proposed buying land cheaply from Indigenous people and reselling it at a high price to settlers. An expedition under Colonel William Wakefield on the ship Tory offered guns, tools and clothing around what is now Wellington, and by November had marks on deeds that supposedly covered 20 million acres, at about a halfpenny an acre. The 1840 Treaty of Waitangi then gave the British Crown the sole right to buy Māori land, and Governor Hobson began reviewing all earlier sales. A land commission under William Spain, set up by the Colonial Office, found serious flaws, including chiefs who had not been consulted. A disputed purchase in the Wairau Valley led in 1843 to a clash in which 22 settlers and four Māori died. Financial trouble began that year. The company returned its charter in 1850 and closed in 1858, having founded Wellington, Nelson, Wanganui and Dunedin.
mechanism: A private company tried to buy land before the state arrived, and the treaty then made the Crown the only lawful buyer. Its deeds were reviewed and could not stand on their own.

name: Sazan and Zvërnec resort plan
founder: Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump, with investors
challenge: Court challenges, street protests and a prosecutors’ freeze on a partner firm
recognition: Preliminary approval from the Albanian government
story: Sazan is an uninhabited island off Albania's Adriatic coast, once a Soviet submarine base, and Zvërnec is the strip of beach and lagoon opposite it. Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump, the son-in-law and daughter of US President Donald Trump, plan a luxury resort there. In 2026 Ivanka Trump described both as belonging to them, including five miles of beachfront. Albania's government has given preliminary approval. The coast lies in the protected Vjosa-Narta area, home to about 250 bird species. In 2024 Prime Minister Edi Rama brought in a law allowing five-star hotels there, and environmental groups have gone to court, arguing that it breaks Albanian and European Union law. In June 2026 thousands protested in Tirana for days, with some saying the government was selling land that was not its to sell. That month prosecutors froze the accounts of a firm owned by the Qatari brothers Moutaz and Ramez Al-Khayyat, who are helping finance the project, in an inquiry into fraudulent land titles. A representative said Kushner's Affinity Partners has no role and that partners invest personally. A journalist tracing the ownership found a chain of shell companies.
mechanism: A government can open protected public land to private developers by changing its law. Sovereignty stays Albanian, and the dispute is over who had the right to give the land away.

sources.t: In Albania, anger grows against the government for supporting a Kushner-linked luxury resort, NPR via KPBS

name: Petition for Denmark to buy California
cost: A joke goal of $1 trillion, with no money collected
story: In February 2025 a satirical online petition called on Denmark to buy the American state of California, as a reply to President Trump's repeated demands for Greenland, a territory of Denmark. The site, Denmarkification, set a goal of crowdfunding $1 trillion, joked about renaming Disneyland and sending Lego executives to negotiate, and argued that Trump would sell because he had called California "the most ruined state in the Union". It collected over 200,000 signatures by its own count, though The Local said that figure might be part of the joke. It took signatures only, not money. Its authors were unknown.
mechanism: A petition has no legal effect on territory. This one was written to mock the demand to buy Greenland.

sources.t: Petition for Denmark to buy California for $1 trillion surpasses 200,000 signatures, CBS

name: Puertopia or Sol
anchor: San Juan, where the group was based.
founder: Brock Pierce and fellow cryptocurrency investors
story: Puertopia, later renamed Sol, was a plan by wealthy cryptocurrency investors to build a new city in Puerto Rico, a US territory, in which the money would be virtual and contracts public. They arrived after Hurricane Maria in September 2017, drawn by tax rules that spare residents federal income tax and capital gains tax. Their leader was Brock Pierce, director of the Bitcoin Foundation and co-founder of the blockchain firm Block.One. In early 2018 they toured properties and debated buying the Roosevelt Roads Naval Station, 9,000 acres with two deep-water ports. Another resident said they had told him they would buy 250,000 acres and incorporate their own city. Some members thought moving into Old San Juan was enough. A local critic spoke of crypto colonialism, and another Puerto Rican called the island a tax playground for the rich. No report says that they bought the base or founded a city.
mechanism: Puerto Rico's tax rules can be used without any land deal, and buying land there brings no separate sovereignty, because the island remains under United States law. The investors' plan relied on those rules and on local government goodwill.

sources.t: Welcome to Puertopia, a Caribbean crypto-paradise, The Irish Times
